The opening clue

Someone has taken the stars out of a stellar nursery. Look at the assigned APOD image: red clouds curl around a blue centre, while dark fingers reach across the glow. It looks busy, but the objects we came to find are missing. Has the Eagle Nebula somehow lost its stars?

The answer is in the processing. The stars were digitally removed; their physical surroundings remain. This particular photograph makes the material between stars unusually easy to notice (Nemiroff and Bonnell, 2022). Think of it as the first clue in an investigation: what can the clouds tell us about the stars we cannot see?

This investigation asks how astronomers recognise stellar birth when a photograph can hide its stars. Following the Eagle Nebula from a processed image to infrared observations connects three ideas from astronomy: gravity gathers material, fusion powers mature stars, and light carries evidence of both. Each view answers a different part of the puzzle.

01 / Read the scene

The stars left
the photograph.

The material they formed from is still here. Open the assigned APOD to examine the original, then select a clue.

A glow with a source

Hot stars can energise surrounding gas. The gas can glow even after the stars are digitally removed from the displayed image. See NASA (n.d.b).

The Eagle Nebula, also called M16, lies roughly 6,500 light-years away in the direction of Serpens. A light-year measures distance: its light has travelled for about 6,500 years before reaching us. Figure 1 therefore offers a delayed view of a distant region, rather than a live picture of what it looks like today (Nemiroff and Bonnell, 2022).

Look again at the bright centre. The APOD explanation describes a cavity within a larger dusty structure, with dense pillars and globules remaining inside. The image combines selected emissions from hydrogen, displayed in red, and oxygen, displayed in blue, gathered over more than 22 hours of imaging. Those colours help separate structures; they do not make this an ordinary snapshot of what your eyes would see (Nemiroff and Bonnell, 2022).

Why does the gas glow at all? Nearby hot stars supply energetic ultraviolet light. That radiation can strip electrons from hydrogen atoms, a process called ionisation. When electrons recombine with the ions and settle into lower energy states, they release light. An emission nebula can therefore reveal the influence of stars even when the stars themselves have been removed from a displayed image (NASA, n.d.b).

The dark features require a different explanation. Dust absorbs and scatters visible light, hiding material behind it. Stellar nurseries contain cold molecular gas, mainly hydrogen with helium, mixed with a small amount of dust. Dense, shielded material can remain cold while exposed gas nearby glows. The dark fingers in Figure 1 therefore need not be empty gaps. Their darkness alone, however, cannot establish that a particular clump contains a protostar (NASA, n.d.b; n.d.e).

02 / Follow the material

Build a star.
Start with a cloud.

Choose a stage or play the schematic. This is a conceptual illustration, not a physical simulation.

A cloud cannot turn into a star merely by looking dramatic. Gravity must overcome support from gas pressure and other effects, including magnetic fields. Cooling reduces thermal pressure, so sufficiently dense, cool regions can collapse. Dust helps radiate energy away. As material contracts, a central concentration grows; its rotation becomes important, and conservation of angular momentum helps explain why infalling material forms an accretion disc rather than all dropping straight into the centre (NASA, n.d.a).

The word accretion simply means growth by collecting material. Imagine following one parcel of gas inward: it joins an increasingly crowded, heated environment rather than falling into an empty hole. In Figure 2, the stages are separated so the process is readable. Real clouds can fragment, and stars may develop together rather than follow a single isolated sequence (NASA, n.d.a).

The growing object is a protostar. It can already shine: as gravity draws material inward, gravitational potential energy is converted into heat and radiation. Seeing a luminous young object therefore does not automatically tell us that it has reached the same life stage as the Sun (NASA, n.d.e).

If its core eventually becomes hot and dense enough, sustained hydrogen fusion begins. Hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium, releasing energy. This is the start of the main-sequence phase. The Sun is in this phase today. Energy flowing outward helps maintain the internal pressure that balances gravity, allowing a star to remain stable for a long part of its life (NASA, n.d.d; n.d.e).

Figure 2 separates these energy sources into readable stages. A real cloud can fragment into multiple stars, whose masses influence their futures: massive stars consume their fuel much faster and have shorter lives. The drawing describes a possible pathway for material in a nursery such as M16; it does not track a measured clump in Figure 1 or provide a clock for its evolution (NASA, n.d.a; n.d.e).

The nursery has some difficult neighbours

A new star changes its surroundings. Massive young stars can be especially influential: their intense radiation affects nearby gas, while stellar winds carry material outward. In the Pillars of Creation, radiation and winds from nearby massive stars erode the gas and dust. The pillars may resemble permanent stone monuments, yet they are structures in material that is being altered (ESA, 2015).

Picture a sand sculpture in a strong wind, with one qualification: these pillars are clouds, and both radiation and moving particles act on them. The comparison helps explain why shape alone cannot promise permanence. A pillar can provide material for star formation while its exposed surroundings are being dispersed (ESA, 2015).

Feedback is the name for stars influencing the material around them. Radiation and winds may remove material that could have fed new stars, while compression can sometimes help other regions collapse. The outcome depends on the local conditions. We cannot decide from a striking outline alone that a particular bright rim has triggered a new generation of stars (NASA, n.d.a; n.d.b).

03 / Change the detector

Different light.
A different cast.

Webb's near-infrared and mid-infrared instruments emphasise different parts of the same star-forming region.

Now give the investigation a different instrument. Figure 3 shows the Pillars of Creation within the Eagle Nebula, observed by the James Webb Space Telescope's Near-Infrared Camera, NIRCam. Released on 19 October 2022, this field spans about eight light-years: even light would need roughly eight years to cross that width. This is the image field, not the size of the entire nebula. Its framing differs from Figure 1 (NASA, 2022c).

The published images differ in framing and scale. These are not aligned overlays, and the assigned APOD covers a wider scene.

What Webb revealed in 2022

Near-infrared light has wavelengths longer than visible light and can pass through some dusty regions more readily. Webb therefore reveals stars and structures that are harder to see at visible wavelengths. It does not make every cloud transparent. The image is assembled from several infrared filters, with visible colours assigned to their data so that we can inspect the result (NASA, 2022c).

The 2022 release reports a concrete observation: bright red orbs, typically with diffraction spikes outside the dusty pillars, are newly formed stars. Wavy red features near some pillar edges trace outflows from stars still forming. Their jets strike surrounding gas, producing shocks and emission from energetic molecular hydrogen. The apparent lava is not molten rock. These details connect Figure 3 to active stellar birth rather than merely to an impressive cloud shape (NASA, 2022b).

Why does this matter? Identifying young stars and measuring their surroundings allows astronomers to test models of how clouds become stellar populations. NASA describes improved star counts and gas and dust estimates as a use of these observations; the release does not itself establish an exact star-formation rate. Nor is 2022 the birth date of the stars: it dates the published observation (NASA, 2022b).

Why stars can look absent again

Here is a twist. Figure 4 also comes from Webb, but its Mid-Infrared Instrument, MIRI, gives the pillars a different appearance. Far fewer stars stand out. Has somebody removed them again?

This time the explanation is wavelength. MIRI is particularly effective at showing dust emission, while many stars are too faint in these bands to dominate the scene. Some young objects still surrounded by dusty material remain noticeable. The change between Figures 3 and 4 illustrates how the light an instrument measures determines which parts of a nebula stand out (NASA, 2022a).

Keep three explanations separate. In Figure 1, stars were removed during processing. Along dusty sightlines, light can be obscured before it reaches a telescope. In Figure 4, the balance of stellar and dust emission changes with the observing bands. Comparing these images therefore requires their captions and observing information, not just counting the bright points on the page (Nemiroff and Bonnell, 2022; NASA, 2022a).

Missing from a processed image, hidden by dust, or faint in the observing band: three different explanations can produce an apparently missing star.

04 / Check your interpretation

Ready to close
the case?

Try three questions before reading the conclusion. You can change an answer and check again.

Why are stars absent from the assigned APOD image?

Does a dark clump prove that a star is forming inside?

Why do fewer stars stand out in the MIRI view?

What the pictures cannot decide for us

There is a further limit to this investigation: the images flatten a three-dimensional region onto a page. Apparent neighbours need not share the same depth. The assigned colours also prevent us from treating every red point as a temperature measurement. Figure 3 combines several filters; physical interpretation depends on those measurements and supporting evidence, not the display colour alone (NASA, 2022c).

Astronomers can also spread light into a spectrum. Patterns of emission and absorption reveal information about composition, temperature and motion that a colour photograph does not provide on its own. Spectroscopy therefore offers additional ways to examine an interpretation suggested by an image (NASA, n.d.c).

Return to the original puzzle. The Eagle Nebula did not need to lose its stars for us to see it differently. Removing them from one photograph directed our attention to their surroundings; changing wavelengths then revealed different evidence within those surroundings. The next time a space image stops you scrolling, look beyond the colours. Ask which light was recorded, what was processed, and what remains hidden. Those questions are a useful beginning to doing astronomy.
